w: 1 CAL = PD + recession, with its sign: negative recession in Salud A professor's hint · 6 questions in the bank Know this The margin sits coronal to the CEJ, so recession is negative. CAL = PD + GR with its sign: PD 5, GR −3 → CAL 2. In Salud a blank or a reflexive 0 sets CAL = PD. Skipped negative recession turns a CAL-2 site into CAL 5 and a false Stage 3/4. The lecture's main point about these numbers: in health, probing depth is not equal to clinical attachment level. In intact tissue the gingival margin sits slightly coronal to the CEJ and hides it. Recession is positive when there is true recession (you can see the CEJ) and negative when the margin is coronal to the CEJ: −1, −2, −3, or −3 to −4 or more with drug-induced overgrowth. Add it with its sign. PD 5 mm with GR −3 mm gives CAL 2 mm. Skip the recession and that same site reads CAL 5 mm, which would push you toward Stage 3 or 4 even though the radiographs may show only about 20% bone loss. Probing depth, CAL and the radiographs have to tell the same story. The same trap is built into Salud. Leave recession blank, or type 0 without checking whether it is really positive or negative, and Salud sets CAL equal to PD. A blank over-diagnoses disease, and a reflexive zero gives an inaccurate diagnosis too. Only when you enter the signed value does Salud calculate CAL correctly. 2 The host does 75% of the damage, bacteria 25% A professor's hint · 2 questions in the bank Know this The 25/75 split. Bacteria bring endotoxin (LPS), not osteoclasts. Removing them calms the host, and host modulation (Dr. Litz) calms it directly. SRP targets the bacteria, yet bacteria cause only about 25% of the damage. About 75% comes from the host's inflammatory mediators and bone-destroying cells (osteoclasts). Bacteria bring endotoxin (lipopolysaccharide), not osteoclasts. Removing the bacteria calms the host response. When even good home care plus the best SRP or surgery leaves residual disease, you can also calm the host directly. That is host modulation, or "periodontal medicine," covered later by Dr. Litz. Bacteria cover calculus and live inside its tubules. Calculus and plaque also act as irritants the host reacts to, supra- or subgingivally. 3 Glickman furcation classes; Class II is the most regenerable A professor's hint · 4 questions in the bank Know this Glickman, not millimeters: I catch, II cul-de-sac (containable), III through-and-through, IV visible. Root caries in a Class IV furcation means a hopeless tooth. Class II, cul-de-sac. A definite furcation invasion, but a bony wall remains on the other side (probe from buccal and the palatal or lingual crest is still there). It has depth and containability, so it is the class most amenable to regeneration. Class IV. A class III that has also lost the soft tissue over it, naturally through recession or surgically, so the through-and-through furcation is visible. The patient can clean it with interdental aids or a water flosser, but the exposed root trunk risks sensitivity and root caries. Caries in a furcation makes the tooth hopeless, so keep these teeth under close watch at every maintenance visit. 4 Debridement has one indication and is never combined with SRP A professor's hint · 3 questions in the bank Know this The only indication is calculus hiding the gingival margin so no numbers can be captured. Full-mouth code only; insurance won't pay for it plus an exam the same day (return in about 2 weeks). Debridement is not a therapeutic procedure. You never do it to treat disease, and it should never be combined with scaling and root planing. Its only indication is that calculus hides the gingival margin so completely that you can't see or explore it, and so can't capture any numbers. There is only a full-mouth debridement code. No half-mouth, lower-anterior or maxillary-posterior version exists. The code is intended for generalized calculus heavy enough to cover even chewing surfaces, and you will seldom see that. Insurance won't pay for debridement and a periodontal exam at the same visit, on the reasoning that if you couldn't probe before, the tissue won't be ready right after. So in practice the patient comes back in about two weeks for full charting. 5 What SRP aims for, and re-evaluation at 4-6 weeks A professor's hint · 6 questions in the bank Know this Why re-evaluation is at 4-6 weeks: JE reattaches in 7-10 days, connective tissue in 4-6 weeks (collagen matures over 3-6 months). At re-eval, residual calculus → remove it and re-evaluate in 2 weeks. Otherwise the fix is home care, not more SRP. The healing clock: junctional epithelium 7-10 days, connective tissue reattachment 4-6 weeks, and collagen fiber maturation and orientation 3-6 months. That is why the patient returns at 4-6 weeks. You see the maximum result by then, and research shows waiting longer gives no additional pocket reduction. The deck puts it slightly differently: the biggest PD changes happen in the first 4 weeks, the dentogingival junction is re-established at 2-4 weeks, and repair and maturation can continue for 9-12 months. Know both sets of numbers. The deck's "6 mm might become 5 or 4.5" figures are there for a sense of scale. She said you are not expected to memorize them. Re-evaluate at 4-6 weeks: plaque scores, signs of inflammation, BOP, PD, recession, CAL, mobility, furcation and suppuration. This is the visit where the decision about surgery is made. If there's still inflammation and the numbers haven't improved, check whether residual calculus is the reason. You'll often feel it with the probe while recharting. If it is, remove it (not charged) and do another Phase I evaluation in two weeks. If you already removed all the deposits the first time, more rounds of SRP won't do anything. What works is improving the patient's oral hygiene. 6 Prophylaxis vs maintenance vs D4346 A professor's hint · 5 questions in the bank Know this Prophylaxis is preventive, for patients who never had periodontitis. Maintenance is supportive therapy after treated periodontitis, and localized SRP on residual pockets falls under it. D4346 sits between prophy and SRP. Prophylaxis is preventive, not therapeutic. It is for a patient who has never had periodontitis (gingival health or gingivitis). Subgingival calculus doesn't make it periodontitis: normal sulci have depth, and calculus 1-2 mm down is subgingival and gets removed as part of the prophy. Periodontal maintenance is supportive therapy for a patient already treated for periodontitis, to keep the disease from recurring, with oral hygiene evaluated every visit. The terms are not interchangeable. A maintenance patient with mostly 1-3 mm pockets, some residual 4s and an isolated 5 is fine to stay on maintenance when hygiene is good, those sites don't bleed, the tissue looks healthy and the radiographs show no progression. Localized SRP on residual pockets that didn't respond is defined as part of maintenance. Scaling in the presence of gingival inflammation (D4346) sits between a prophy and SRP. It is for a patient never diagnosed with periodontitis who has no bone loss but heavy, generalized inflammation from local factors (plaque and calculus), so a simple prophy undersells the work. At school it's done the perio way, with perio faculty or a resident, and gets a Phase I evaluation. The class case was a young patient (20s to early 30s) with a lingual bridge of calculus. What looked like bone loss around the premolars and mesial of the molars came from second premolars extracted for orthodontics and the tipping that followed, not from periodontitis. Diagnosis: generalized gingival inflammation on a reduced periodontium in a non-periodontitis patient (the deck calls it gingivitis on a reduced periodontium), treated with D4346. That case had debridement, charting and therapy in the same visit. Full-mouth debridement (D4355) is gross removal so a proper evaluation can be done at a later visit. 7 Fremitus is palpated; Miller mobility classes A professor's hint · 5 questions in the bank Know this Fremitus is mobility in function, felt with a finger on the root; it can be vertical and/or horizontal. Static mobility uses two blunt instruments, and a depressible tooth is ready for extraction. Mobility is checked with two rigid (blunt) instruments, one on each side of the tooth, and graded on the Miller scale: 0 is normal, 1 is slightly more than normal (<1 mm), 2 is moderately more (>1 mm but <2 mm), and 3 is severe faciolingual and/or mesiodistal mobility combined with vertical displacement. A tooth that is depressible in its socket is ready for extraction. That's static mobility. Fremitus is mobility in function. You rest a finger on the root while the patient brings the teeth together and feel for vibration. It can have a vertical and/or horizontal component, and it is palpated, not seen, unless it is extreme. Positive fremitus means you need to find out why the tooth carries that load. In the class example, lack of posterior support meant the premolars were doing the work of molars. 8 Instrumentation: finger rests, scaling vs root planing, what the ultrasonic can't do A professor's hint · 4 questions in the bank Know this Piezoelectric units work subgingivally too. Her sequence: ultrasonic for gross deposits → hand instruments → ultrasonic again for lavage. The clinic has piezoelectric ultrasonic handpieces and tips alongside hand instruments. They can be used subgingivally, but they cannot root plane, so they won't leave a smooth root. Use them in combination: ultrasonic to remove gross deposits, then hand instruments, then the ultrasonic again so the irrigation's lavage flushes the pocket. There are four intraoral finger rests: conventional (tooth surfaces right next to the working area), cross-arch (the other side of the same arch), opposite-arch (the opposite arch), and finger-on-finger (the index finger or thumb of the non-working hand). Adaptation depends on the tissue (fibrotic vs. hemorrhagic), the severity of disease (how retractable the tissue is, the interproximal embrasure), and how tenacious the calculus is. Also flagged in class The one slide in the deck set in all-caps emphasis. Know the four finger rests (conventional, cross-arch, opposite-arch, finger-on-finger). From the slide deck. In class she deferred grasp and finger rests to the PCD sessions, so expect them there and on the practical. Said of the host-bacteria pathogenesis diagram (health → gingivitis → periodontitis). Know it cold: plaque bacteria initiate, the host response drives progression, and SRP targets the bacteria. Occlusal trauma on a reduced periodontium (lack of posterior support, parafunction, overjet/overbite). Record occlusal findings in the notes section, since the chart has no field for them. The goals are less inflammation, a gram-negative → gram-positive shift and arrested progression. SRP does not reverse bone or attachment loss, even though PD drops. Scaling is supra- and subgingival. Root planing is subgingival, on root surfaces only. Clinically they're done together. Radiographs show bone loss (localized/generalized, horizontal/vertical), tipping, fused roots, root proximity, calculus, the sinus and PA lesions. Keep them open during SRP rather than the chart.
